alabama.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage)
alabama.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage, from the moment a ride is accepted until the passenger is dropped off
alabama.sol_note: The two-year clock under Ala. Code § 6-2-38 starts on the date of the crash, is tolled while the injured person is a minor, and claims against a city require written notice within 6 months.
alabama.sources: Ala. Code § 32-7C-2 (Justia), Ala. Code § 32-7C-22, Alabama Public Service Commission TNC page, Ala. Code § 6-2-38
alabama.state_note: Alabama's TNC law (2018) requires every TNC to hold a permit from the Public Service Commission, and the statute bars any contract between a TNC and its drivers or riders from reducing the required insurance. The Commission also runs a TNC complaint process and requires a zero-tolerance drug and alcohol policy.
alabama.tnc_statute: Alabama Code §§ 32-7C-1 to 32-7C-36 (Transportation Network Company Act); insurance requirements at Ala. Code § 32-7C-2
alabama.um_uim_note: No separate UM/UIM amount is set for rideshare in the TNC statute; the statute requires all other state-mandated motor vehicle coverage, and Alabama law requires UM coverage to be offered at minimum limits of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident, though a driver may reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies.
alabama.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While the driver is logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver's personal policy is first in line if it covers TNC activity, but most personal policies exclude commercial use, and Alabama law requires the TNC's coverage to step in from the first dollar if the driver's policy lapses or does not cover the claim. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first regardless of the driver's personal coverage.

alaska.agency_name: Alaska Department of Administration, Division of Motor Vehicles
alaska.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage)
alaska.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car)
alaska.sol_note: The two-year clock under AS 09.10.070 starts on the date of the crash, or when the injury was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and is tolled while the injured person is a minor.
alaska.sources: Alaska Stat. § 28.23.050 (Justia), Alaska Stat. § 21.96.018, Alaska Stat. § 28.23.110, Alaska Stat. § 09.10.070
alaska.state_note: Alaska's TNC law (2017) requires no state TNC permit or registration; companies must comply with the statute's insurance, background-check, and vehicle-inspection rules on their own. Distinctive rules: a TNC vehicle may be no more than 12 years old, and drivers are independent contractors by statute (AS 28.23.080).
alaska.tnc_statute: Alaska Statutes §§ 28.23.010-28.23.180 (Transportation Network Companies and Drivers); insurance at AS 28.23.050 and AS 21.96.018
alaska.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required in both periods as required by AS 21.96.020 and AS 28.20.440, at Alaska's minimums of $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident; Alaska law requires UM coverage to be offered but allows the policyholder to reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies.
alaska.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver's personal policy pays first if it covers TNC driving, but Alaska law expressly lets personal insurers exclude all coverage while a driver is logged on or giving a prearranged ride. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar and defend the claim, and the TNC's coverage may not be conditioned on the personal insurer denying the claim first. During a prearranged ride (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays.

arizona.agency_name: Arizona Department of Transportation, Motor Vehicle Division
arizona.period1_limits: $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident for bodily injury or death, $20,000 property damage (state statutory minimum; Uber and Lyft in practice provide higher Period 1 limits of $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident, with $25,000 property damage from Uber and $20,000 from Lyft)
arizona.period2_3_limits: Period 2 (en route to pickup): $250,000 per incident primary commercial liability. Period 3 (passenger in the vehicle): $1,000,000 per incident primary commercial liability (raised from $250,000 by HB 2729 in 2024).
arizona.sol_note: The two-year clock under A.R.S. § 12-542 starts on the date of the crash, or when the injury was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and a claim against a public entity requires a notice of claim within 180 days.
arizona.sources: A.R.S. § 28-4038, A.R.S. § 28-9552, Arizona Senate Fact Sheet for HB 2729 (2024), Arizona Department of Transportation Vehicle for Hire Licensing page, A.R.S. § 12-542
arizona.state_note: Arizona is unusual in splitting Periods 2 and 3: the $1,000,000 floor applies only once a passenger is in the car, while the drive to the pickup is capped at a $250,000 statutory minimum (though Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 for both periods under their own policies). TNCs must hold an ADOT permit, drivers must be at least 19, and public airports may still regulate TNC pickups.
arizona.tnc_statute: Arizona Revised Statutes Title 28, Chapter 30, §§ 28-9551 et seq. (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at A.R.S. § 28-4038
arizona.um_uim_note: Arizona requires commercial UM coverage in the rideshare context: $250,000 per incident while the driver is en route to a pickup, and $25,000 per person / $75,000 per incident while a passenger is in the vehicle (A.R.S. § 28-4038, as amended by HB 2729 in 2024). Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies, above the state floor.
arizona.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), coverage may come from the driver's policy, the TNC's policy, or a combination, and the TNC must provide coverage from the first dollar if the driver's policy excludes TNC activity or falls short. Once a ride is accepted, the TNC's commercial policy is primary: $250,000 while en route to the pickup and $1,000,000 once a passenger is in the car. Most personal auto policies exclude driving for hire, so a personal insurer's denial is common and does not leave the injured person without coverage in Periods 2 and 3.

arkansas.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage)
arkansas.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car)
arkansas.sol_note: The three-year clock under Ark. Code § 16-56-105 starts on the date of the crash and is tolled while the injured person is a minor.
arkansas.sources: Ark. Code § 23-13-709 (Justia), Ark. Code §§ 23-13-701 to 23-13-719, Arkansas Public Service Commission TNC page, Ark. Code § 16-56-105
arkansas.state_note: Arkansas was an early TNC regulator (2015): every TNC must hold a permit from the Public Service Commission, and Arkansas gives crash victims three years to file, longer than most states in this set. The statute also states that a TNC driver is an independent contractor, not an employee of the company.
arkansas.tnc_statute: Arkansas Code §§ 23-13-701 to 23-13-719 (Transportation Network Company Services Act); insurance requirements at Ark. Code § 23-13-709
arkansas.um_uim_note: The TNC statute does not set a separate UM/UIM amount for rideshare; Arkansas law requires UM coverage to be offered at minimum limits of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident, and a driver may reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies.
arkansas.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver's policy pays first if it covers TNC driving, but the TNC must provide coverage from the first dollar if the driver's policy excludes the activity or does not meet the minimums. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Most personal policies exclude driving for hire, so a personal insurer's denial is common and triggers the TNC's first-dollar duty.

california.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and personal injury, $30,000 property damage (primary coverage), plus $200,000 per occurrence in excess coverage
california.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, personal injury, and property damage from the moment a ride is accepted until the ride is complete
california.sol_note: The two-year clock under Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1 starts on the date of the crash, or when the injury was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and a claim against a government entity requires a written claim within 6 months.
california.sources: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5433 (California Legislative Information), Cal. Pub. Util. Code §§ 5430-5445, California Public Utilities Commission TNC permits page, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 335.1, SB 371 (Stats. 2025, ch. 314)
california.state_note: California created the TNC category and is the only state in this set where the regulator (the CPUC) issues TNC permits and sets detailed rules in General Order 157. Proposition 22 (2020) keeps rideshare drivers as independent contractors, and California's $30,000 Period 1 property-damage floor is higher than the $25,000 used in most other states.
california.tnc_statute: California Public Utilities Code §§ 5430-5445, Article 7 (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5433
california.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage of $60,000 per person / $300,000 per incident is required while a passenger is in the vehicle, under Public Utilities Code § 5433(b)(2) as amended by SB 371 (2025), effective January 1, 2026; this is a sharp cut from the $1,000,000 UM/UIM floor that applied before. Uber and Lyft still advertise $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies, above the new state floor.
california.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the TNC's coverage is primary at $50,000/$100,000/$30,000, with $200,000 in excess coverage on top. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary commercial policy pays first. California law requires the TNC to tell drivers in writing that their personal policy may not cover TNC driving, and most personal policies exclude it, so a personal insurer's denial is expected and does not block the TNC coverage.

colorado.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $30,000 property damage (primary coverage)
colorado.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability per occurrence while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car)
colorado.sol_note: Colorado's general personal injury limit is 2 years, but motor vehicle accident injuries get 3 years under C.R.S. § 13-80-101(1)(n), starting on the date of the crash, and a claim against a government entity requires notice within 182 days.
colorado.sources: C.R.S. § 40-10.1-604 (Justia/FindLaw), Colorado Public Utilities Commission TNC consumer page, C.R.S. § 13-80-101(1)(n)
colorado.state_note: Colorado was the first state in the country to regulate TNCs (SB 14-125, 2014), and it has one of the strongest rideshare UM mandates in this set at $200,000 per person / $400,000 per occurrence during a ride. SB 24-075 added fare-transparency and driver-pay rules enforced by the Department of Labor and Employment.
colorado.tnc_statute: Colorado Revised Statutes §§ 40-10.1-601 to 40-10.1-608 (Transportation Network Company Act); insurance requirements at C.R.S. § 40-10.1-604
colorado.um_uim_note: UM coverage of at least $200,000 per person / $400,000 per occurrence is required for the driver and each rider during a prearranged ride, under C.R.S. § 40-10.1-604(2.5), in effect since August 10, 2022. No UM coverage is required during Period 1, so UM protection while waiting depends on the driver's own policy or the TNC's policy terms.
colorado.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies, at Colorado's $25,000/$50,000/$15,000 minimums. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage of $50,000/$100,000/$30,000 that recognizes TNC driving. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Colorado law states that nothing in the TNC statute requires a personal policy to cover time logged into the app, so a personal insurer's denial for commercial use is common and the TNC coverage fills the gap.

connecticut.agency_name: Connecticut Department of Transportation, Regulatory and Compliance Unit
connecticut.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident for bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage)
connecticut.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability per accident for bodily injury, death, or property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car)
connecticut.sol_note: The two-year clock under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-584 starts on the date of the crash or when the injury was discovered, with a three-year outer limit from the act or omission, and a claim against the state requires notice within 1 year.
connecticut.sources: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 13b-120 (Justia), Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 13b-116 to 13b-120, Connecticut Department of Transportation Regulatory and Compliance Unit page, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-584
connecticut.state_note: Connecticut is one of the few states where the transportation department, not a utilities commission, registers TNCs: each company registers annually with the Commissioner of Transportation, paying $5,000, $10,000, or $30,000 depending on how many drivers it has on the platform.
connecticut.tnc_statute: Connecticut General Statutes §§ 13b-116 to 13b-120, Chapter 244c (Transportation Network Company Vehicles); insurance requirements at Conn. Gen. Stat. § 13b-120
connecticut.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required in both periods under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 38a-336, at Connecticut's minimums of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies, above the state floor.
connecticut.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage of $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 plus UM/UIM, and the TNC's coverage steps in from the first dollar if the driver's policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Connecticut law preserves personal-policy exclusions for vehicles used to carry passengers for a fee, so a personal insurer's denial for commercial use is common.

delaware.agency_name: Delaware Department of Transportation, Division of Motor Vehicles
delaware.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage), plus PIP at the minimums in 21 Del. C. § 2118
delaware.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car)
delaware.sol_note: The two-year clock under 10 Del. C. § 8119 starts on the date of the crash, but extends to 3 years if the injury was not discoverable within 2 years, and is tolled while the injured person is a minor.
delaware.sources: 2 Del. C. § 1908 (Justia), 2 Del. C. §§ 1901-1910, 2 Del. Admin. Code § 2289 (Transportation Network Companies), 10 Del. C. § 8119
delaware.state_note: Delaware stands out for its $1,000,000 UM/UIM requirement during a ride — no other state in this set mandates UM that high. TNCs must obtain a permit from the Delaware Department of Transportation and pay a $5,000 annual permit fee.
delaware.tnc_statute: 2 Delaware Code §§ 1901-1910, Chapter 19 (Transportation Networks); insurance requirements at 2 Del. C. § 1908; regulations at 2 Del. Admin. Code § 2289
delaware.um_uim_note: Delaware requires UM/UIM coverage of at least $100,000 per incident during Period 1 and at least $1,000,000 per incident during a prearranged ride (2 Del. C. § 1908) — the highest rideshare UM mandate in this set, matching the $1,000,000 liability limit during a ride.
delaware.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage of $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 plus PIP and $100,000 in UM/UIM. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first, with $1,000,000 in UM/UIM. If the driver's insurance has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar and defend the claim, so a personal insurer's denial for commercial use does not leave the injured person uncovered.

florida.agency_name: Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (no state TNC permit; Fla. Stat. § 627.748 preempts local TNC regulation)
florida.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage (primary coverage), plus PIP at the state no-fault minimums and UM/UIM as required by Fla. Stat. § 627.727
florida.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury, and property damage while the driver is engaged in a prearranged ride (en route to pickup and passenger in the car), plus PIP at the minimums required of a limousine and UM/UIM as required by Fla. Stat. § 627.727
florida.sol_note: The two-year clock under Fla. Stat. § 95.11(5)(a) starts on the date of the crash; HB 837 (2023) cut the negligence limit from 4 years to 2 for claims accruing after March 24, 2023, and claims against a government entity require notice within 180 days.
florida.sources: Fla. Stat. § 627.748 (Justia), Fla. Stat. § 627.727, Fla. Stat. § 95.11(5)(a), Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles
florida.state_note: Florida issues no TNC permit and bars cities and counties from regulating rideshare companies, so the insurance statute is the main state-level control. Because Florida is a no-fault state, PIP coverage is part of the required rideshare insurance in every period, which is not the case in the other states in this set.
florida.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required in both periods as required by Fla. Stat. § 627.727, which requires UM to be offered at limits matching the liability coverage purchased, though a driver may reject it in writing. Uber and Lyft provide $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2 and 3 under their own policies.
florida.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage of $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 plus PIP and UM/UIM, and the TNC's coverage steps in from the first dollar if the driver's policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Florida is a no-fault state, so an injured person's own PIP pays first for medical bills up to its limits regardless of fault, and most personal policies exclude driving for hire, so a personal insurer's denial is common.

georgia.agency_name: Georgia Department of Public Safety, Motor Carrier Compliance Division
georgia.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident for bodily injury or death, $50,000 property damage (primary coverage, per O.C.G.A. § 33-1-24(b)(2); Uber and Lyft's own policy summaries list $25,000 property damage for this period, below the statutory figure)
georgia.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability per occurrence for death, personal injury, and property damage from the moment a ride is accepted until the ride is complete (en route to pickup and passenger in the car)
georgia.sol_note: The two-year clock under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 starts on the date of the crash and is tolled while the injured person is a minor, and a claim against a city or county requires ante-litem notice within 12 months.
georgia.sources: O.C.G.A. § 33-1-24, HB 529 (Ga. 2023), O.C.G.A. § 40-1-201 (HB 339, 2025), Georgia Department of Public Safety Motor Carrier Compliance Division, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33
georgia.state_note: Georgia cut the required rideshare UM/UIM limit from $1,000,000 to $100,000 per person / $300,000 per accident in 2023, and in 2025 HB 339 (O.C.G.A. § 40-1-201) shielded rideshare companies from vicarious liability when the only link to the driver is operating the app — so claims after a crash now focus on the driver's negligence and the TNC's insurance, not on the company itself.
georgia.tnc_statute: O.C.G.A. §§ 40-1-190 to 40-1-201 (Ride Share Network Services); insurance requirements at O.C.G.A. § 33-1-24
georgia.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage of at least $100,000 per person / $300,000 per accident is required during a prearranged ride under O.C.G.A. § 33-1-24(b)(3), as amended by HB 529 (2023), effective for claims accruing on or after July 1, 2023; before that date the required UM/UIM limit was $1,000,000. No UM/UIM amount is set for Period 1, so UM protection while waiting depends on the driver's own policy.
georgia.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. While logged on and waiting (Period 1), the TNC must maintain a primary policy of $50,000/$100,000/$50,000 that recognizes the driver as a TNC driver. Once a ride is accepted and while a passenger is in the car (Periods 2 and 3), the TNC's $1,000,000 primary policy pays first. Most personal auto policies exclude driving for hire, so a personal insurer's denial is common; the TNC's primary policy is what covers the crash in Periods 2 and 3 regardless of the personal policy.

hawaii.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage per accident, plus personal injury protection (PIP) at the $10,000 minimum, with defense costs outside the limits
hawaii.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage per accident, plus PIP at the $10,000 minimum, with defense costs outside the limit
hawaii.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, and it is paused while the injured person is a minor.
hawaii.sources: Haw. Rev. Stat. section 431:10C-703, Haw. Rev. Stat. section 657-7, Hawaii Public Utilities Commission
hawaii.state_note: Hawaii is a no-fault state, so PIP applies in both periods, and defense costs sit outside the liability limits. TNCs are licensed by the Public Utilities Commission or a county agency, and Honolulu has its own TNC driver rules.
hawaii.tnc_statute: Hawaii Revised Statutes sections 431:10C-701 to 431:10C-703 (Transportation Network Companies, part of the motor vehicle insurance chapter)
hawaii.um_uim_note: The TNC statute itself sets no separate UM/UIM dollar amount; Hawaii law requires insurers to offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage under Haw. Rev. Stat. section 431:10C-301, which a driver may reject in writing, and Uber and Lyft provide UM/UIM commercially during a ride.
hawaii.who_pays_note: In Period 1 the required primary coverage may be carried by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of the two. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurer must provide it beginning with the first dollar of the claim and defend the claim. A driver's personal insurer may exclude coverage while the car is used for TNC driving, which is why the TNC must disclose that risk in writing.

idaho.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage
idaho.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage per incident
idaho.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, with only a narrow discovery rule, and it is paused while the injured person is a minor.
idaho.sources: Idaho Code sections 41-2518, 41-2519, 41-2521, Idaho Code section 5-219(4), Idaho Code section 41-2502, Idaho Department of Insurance
idaho.state_note: Idaho has no TNC permit or licensing system; its TNC law is insurance-only and sits in the insurance code. Unusually, the TNC's coverage does not depend on the driver's personal insurer first denying the claim.
idaho.tnc_statute: Idaho Code sections 41-2518 to 41-2521 (Financial Responsibility of Transportation Network Companies and Drivers)
idaho.um_uim_note: The TNC statute sets no UM/UIM amount. Idaho Code section 41-2502 requires UM/UIM coverage to be offered at the state minimum limits, but a named insured may reject either coverage in writing; Uber and Lyft provide UM/UIM commercially during a ride.
idaho.who_pays_note: In both periods the required primary coverage may be carried by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of the two. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it beginning with the first dollar of a claim and defend it, and the TNC's coverage does not depend on the personal insurer first denying the claim. A driver's personal insurer may exclude all coverage, including UM/UIM, while the driver is logged on or on a prearranged ride.

illinois.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and personal injury, $25,000 property damage, with the TNC carrying contingent coverage at the same limits
illinois.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, personal injury and property damage
illinois.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, with a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered at once; a claim against a local government vehicle requires notice within 1 year.
illinois.sources: 625 ILCS 57/10 (Transportation Network Providers Act), 735 ILCS 5/13-202, Illinois Commerce Commission
illinois.state_note: The Transportation Network Providers Act is scheduled to be repealed on September 1, 2028. Chicago layers on its own rules, including a chauffeur license for TNC drivers, and the Act sets a floor that cities may make stricter but not more lenient.
illinois.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Providers Act, 625 ILCS 57/1 et seq., section 57/10 (Insurance)
illinois.um_uim_note: Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage of $50,000 is required only while a passenger is in the vehicle, from the moment the passenger enters until the passenger exits; no UM/UIM amount is set for Period 1.
illinois.who_pays_note: In Period 1 the driver's own policy is first, and the TNC's contingent $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 coverage applies if the driver's policy excludes TNC use or falls short of those limits. In Periods 2 and 3 the TNC's $1,000,000 policy is primary and does not depend on the driver's personal insurer first denying the claim. A personal insurer may deny a claim because the car was being used commercially, which is exactly the gap the contingent and primary TNC coverage is meant to close.

indiana.agency_name: Indiana Department of Revenue, Motor Carrier Services
indiana.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $50,000 per incident property damage (property damage rose from $25,000 to $50,000 on July 1, 2024)
indiana.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 per incident for death, bodily injury and property damage, including uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage of $1,000,000
indiana.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, with only a limited discovery rule; a claim against a government entity requires a tort claim notice within 270 days.
indiana.sources: Ind. Code section 8-2.1-19.1-8, as amended by P.L. 215-2023, Ind. Code section 34-11-2-4, Indiana Department of Revenue General Tax Information Bulletin 301
indiana.state_note: Indiana's Period 1 property damage minimum is higher than the usual $25,000: it rose to $50,000 on July 1, 2024. A TNC may not operate in Indiana without a permit from the Department of Revenue.
indiana.tnc_statute: Ind. Code chapter 8-2.1-19.1 (Transportation Network Companies), section 8-2.1-19.1-8 (Motor vehicle insurance requirements)
indiana.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is included in the TNC requirements at the same limits as liability: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident in Period 1 and $1,000,000 per incident in Periods 2 and 3, under Ind. Code section 8-2.1-19.1-8 as amended in 2023.
indiana.who_pays_note: In both periods the required primary coverage may be carried by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of the two. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance steps in from the first dollar. A driver's personal auto insurer may exclude coverage while the driver is logged on to the TNC network, so the TNC policy is often the only coverage in play.

iowa.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage in the amounts required by Iowa Code section 516A.1
iowa.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage in any one accident, plus uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage of $100,000 per accident
iowa.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, with a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered at once, and it is paused while the injured person is a minor.
iowa.sources: Iowa Code chapter 321N, sections 321N.2 and 321N.4, Iowa Code section 614.1(2), Iowa Code section 516A.1, Iowa Department of Transportation
iowa.state_note: Iowa's Period 2 and 3 UM/UIM minimum of $100,000 per accident is set by statute, which is unusual. A TNC needs a permit from the Iowa Department of Transportation, with a $5,000 application fee, and TNCs are governed exclusively by chapter 321N.
iowa.tnc_statute: Iowa Code chapter 321N (Transportation Network Companies), section 321N.4 (Financial responsibility)
iowa.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required in both periods: in Period 1 in the amounts required under Iowa Code section 516A.1, and in Periods 2 and 3 at $100,000 per accident.
iowa.who_pays_note: In Period 1 the TNC must maintain the primary coverage, and it covers the driver if the driver's own coverage does not apply or falls short. In Periods 2 and 3 the TNC or the driver must maintain the $1,000,000 primary coverage. A driver's personal policy may exclude commercial use, so an injured person should look first to the TNC's policy once the app is on.

kansas.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus the minimum UM and personal injury protection coverage required by Kansas law
kansas.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus the minimum UM and personal injury protection coverage required by Kansas law
kansas.sol_note: The clock starts when the injury happens or becomes reasonably discoverable, but no more than 10 years after the act that caused it, and it is paused while the injured person is a minor.
kansas.sources: Kan. Stat. Ann. sections 8-2701, 8-2708, 8-2710, Kan. Stat. Ann. section 60-513, Kansas Corporation Commission
kansas.state_note: Kansas requires a $5,000 annual TNC permit from the Corporation Commission, and the 2015 TNC act took effect only after the legislature overrode the governor's veto.
kansas.tnc_statute: Kansas Transportation Network Company Services Act, Kan. Stat. Ann. sections 8-2701 to 8-2712, section 8-2708 (Insurance)
kansas.um_uim_note: UM coverage is required in both periods: Kan. Stat. Ann. section 8-2708 incorporates the UM requirements of Kan. Stat. Ann. section 40-284 and the personal injury protection requirements of section 40-3107(f) for Period 1 and for a prearranged ride.
kansas.who_pays_note: In both periods the required primary coverage may be carried by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of the two. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it beginning with the first dollar of a claim and defend the claim. Kansas law lets a personal insurer deny coverage while the app is on, under Kan. Stat. Ann. section 8-2710, so the TNC policy is often the only coverage.

kentucky.agency_name: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Department of Vehicle Regulation
kentucky.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Network of Kentucky (Kentucky Justice Online)
kentucky.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage, plus basic reparation (PIP) benefits and uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage
kentucky.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 liability through Uber and Lyft's commercial policies; Kentucky's statutory floor for a prearranged ride under KRS 281.655 is lower, the amounts set for vehicles transporting persons ($100,000 per person / $300,000 per accident / $50,000 property damage for a vehicle with seven or fewer seats), so the $1,000,000 figure is company coverage, not the state minimum
kentucky.sol_note: For a motor vehicle crash, the deadline is 2 years from the injury or from the last basic reparation (PIP) payment, whichever is later, under KRS 304.39-230; Kentucky's general personal injury deadline is only 1 year under KRS 413.140.
kentucky.sources: Ky. Rev. Stat. section 281.655, 601 Ky. Admin. Regs. 1:113, Ky. Rev. Stat. section 304.39-230(6), Ky. Rev. Stat. section 413.140(1)(a), Kentucky Transportation Cabinet
kentucky.state_note: Kentucky is a no-fault state with $10,000 in basic reparation (PIP) benefits, and a person must generally meet a threshold, such as $1,000 in medical expenses, to sue for pain and suffering. TNC insurance is set by both the statute and the Cabinet's regulation, 601 KAR 1:113.
kentucky.tnc_statute: Ky. Rev. Stat. section 281.655 (Transportation network company insurance) and 601 Ky. Admin. Regs. 1:113 (Transportation network company)
kentucky.um_uim_note: UM and UIM coverage are required in both periods: pre-trip coverage includes uninsured vehicle coverage under KRS 304.20-020 and underinsured coverage under KRS 304.39-320, and the same UM/UIM and PIP coverage applies on a prearranged ride.
kentucky.who_pays_note: In Period 1 the TNC must maintain a pre-trip acceptance liability policy, and in Periods 2 and 3 the TNC's primary policy applies. If the driver's own insurance has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC must provide the required coverage beginning with the first dollar and defend the claim. A driver's personal insurer may exclude TNC use, so the TNC policy is usually the coverage that pays.

louisiana.agency_name: Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development
louisiana.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage to the extent required by law
louisiana.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage to the extent required by law
louisiana.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the injury; the period is 2 years for injuries on or after July 1, 2024, and was 1 year for injuries before that date.
louisiana.sources: La. Rev. Stat. sections 45:201.1 to 45:201.14, La. Rev. Stat. section 45:201.6, La. Rev. Stat. sections 48:2191 to 48:2205, La. Civ. Code art. 3493.1, Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development
louisiana.state_note: Louisiana has two TNC laws: the insurance law at La. Rev. Stat. sections 45:201.1-201.14 and the operating/permit law at sections 48:2191-2205. UM coverage can be waived in writing, and Uber has done so in Louisiana, a waiver upheld by the courts, so do not count on company UM coverage here.
louisiana.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Company Motor Vehicle Responsibility Law, La. Rev. Stat. sections 45:201.1 to 45:201.14, section 45:201.6 (Insurance requirements), and La. Rev. Stat. sections 48:2191 to 48:2205 (TNC permits and operations)
louisiana.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required only to the extent required by La. Rev. Stat. section 22:1295, which allows an insured to reject it in writing; Uber executed a valid UM/UIM waiver in Louisiana, upheld in Jean v. James River Insurance Co. and in Guerrera v. United Financial Casualty Co. (5th Cir. 2025), so a crash caused by an uninsured driver may leave no company UM coverage.
louisiana.who_pays_note: In both periods the required primary coverage may be carried by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of the two. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurer must provide the required coverage beginning with the first dollar of a claim and defend it. A driver's personal insurer may exclude any coverage while the driver is logged on or on a prearranged ride, under La. Rev. Stat. section 45:201.7.

maine.agency_name: Maine Secretary of State (Bureau of Motor Vehicles)
maine.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus medical payments coverage and uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage
maine.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus medical payments coverage and uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage
maine.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, with a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered at once; a claim against a government entity requires notice within 180 days under the Maine Tort Claims Act.
maine.sources: 24-A Me. Rev. Stat. section 7303, 29-A Me. Rev. Stat. sections 1672 and 1673, 14 Me. Rev. Stat. section 752, Maine Secretary of State
maine.state_note: Maine has the longest deadline in this set at 6 years. A TNC needs a permit from the Secretary of State costing $10,000 a year, and operating without one is a Class D crime; TNC drivers must be at least 19 years old.
maine.tnc_statute: 24-A Me. Rev. Stat. sections 7301 to 7306 (Transportation Network Company Insurance) and 29-A Me. Rev. Stat. sections 1671 to 1675 (Transportation Network Companies), section 7303 (Financial responsibility)
maine.um_uim_note: UM and UIM coverage are required in both periods under 24-A Me. Rev. Stat. section 7303, in the amounts required by 24-A Me. Rev. Stat. section 2902, plus medical payments coverage under 29-A Me. Rev. Stat. section 1605-A.
maine.who_pays_note: In both periods the required primary coverage may be carried by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of the two. If the driver's coverage has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC must provide the required coverage beginning with the first dollar of a claim and defend it. A driver's personal insurer may exclude all coverage while the driver is logged on or on a prearranged ride, under 24-A Me. Rev. Stat. section 7305.

maryland.period1_limits: $50,000 for bodily injury or death to any one person / $100,000 for two or more persons, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured motorist coverage and personal injury protection
maryland.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 liability in practice through Uber and Lyft's commercial policies, but Maryland law itself only requires $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury or death and $25,000 property damage for all periods, so the $1,000,000 figure is company coverage, not the state minimum
maryland.sol_note: The clock starts when the injury is discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and it is paused while the injured person is a minor; a claim against a local government requires notice within 1 year.
maryland.sources: Md. Code, Public Utilities Article section 10-405, Md. Code Regs. 20.95.01.20, Md. Code, Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article section 5-101, Maryland Public Service Commission
maryland.state_note: Maryland is the outlier here: its statute sets the same $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 floor for all three periods and never rises to $1,000,000 by law. The Commission licenses TNCs and also licenses each driver as a Transportation Network Operator and permits each vehicle, and it has moved against unlicensed rideshare operators such as Empower.
maryland.tnc_statute: Md. Code, Public Utilities Article sections 10-401 to 10-411 (Transportation Network Services), section 10-405 (Insurance or other security), and Md. Code Regs. 20.95.01.20
maryland.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage and personal injury protection are required while the operator is providing transportation network services, under Md. Code, Public Utilities Article section 10-405(a)(2).
maryland.who_pays_note: The operator, the TNC on the operator's behalf, or a combination of both must maintain the required primary coverage, and the driver's own policy is primary where both the driver and the company carry coverage. If the operator's coverage lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance must provide the required coverage from the first dollar of a claim and defend it. A driver's personal insurer may exclude commercial use, so the TNC policy is usually the coverage that pays once the app is on.

massachusetts.agency_name: Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities, Transportation Network Company Division
massachusetts.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per occurrence bodily injury, $30,000 per occurrence property damage
massachusetts.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 per occurrence, per vehicle, for death, bodily injury and property damage
massachusetts.sol_note: The clock normally starts on the crash date under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 2A, with a discovery rule if the injury and its cause could not reasonably have been known, tolling for minors and incapacitated persons, and a shorter 2-year written presentment requirement for claims against the Commonwealth or a public employer.
massachusetts.sources: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 159A 1/2, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 175, § 228, Massachusetts Division of Insurance 2022 TNC Annual Report (mass.gov), Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 2A
massachusetts.state_note: Massachusetts is distinctive in two ways: its Period 1 property-damage minimum is $30,000, not the $25,000 used in most states (some secondary sources wrongly state $25,000; the Division of Insurance annual report and ch. 175, § 228(c) say $30,000), and Massachusetts is a no-fault state, so PIP of at least $8,000 also applies during rideshare periods. Voters also approved a 2024 law (St. 2024, c. 252) giving TNC drivers the option to unionize and bargain collectively.
massachusetts.tnc_statute: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 159A 1/2 (Transportation Network Companies) and Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 175, § 228 (TNC insurance requirements); 220 CMR 274.00
massachusetts.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both Period 1 and Periods 2-3, to the extent required by Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 175, § 113L (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 175, § 228(c)-(d)); Uber and Lyft also provide UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2-3 under their company policies.
massachusetts.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal auto policy applies. In Period 1 the required coverage may be held by the driver, the TNC, or a combination of both, and in practice Uber/Lyft provide contingent coverage at the Period 1 limits. If the driver's own insurance has lapsed, failed to provide the required coverage, or denied the claim, the TNC's insurance must provide the required coverage from the first dollar of the claim and defend it (ch. 175, § 228(e)), so a personal-insurer denial for commercial use does not leave the injured person without coverage while the driver is logged on.

michigan.agency_name: Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), Corporations, Securities and Commercial Licensing Bureau
michigan.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus PIP and property protection insurance as required by the Insurance Code
michigan.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 combined single limit for all bodily injury or property damage, plus PIP and property protection insurance as required by the Insurance Code
michigan.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the injury under MCL 600.5805(2), with tolling for minors, but no-fault PIP benefit claims have a separate 1-year deadline under MCL 500.3145 and claims against a public transit authority can require written notice within 60 days.
michigan.state_note: Michigan's no-fault system makes it distinctive: TNCs must elect higher PIP levels ($250,000, $500,000, or unlimited), yet an injured passenger's own PIP policy is usually the first payer, with the TNC's PIP applying only when no other policy is available. Michigan also requires an annual vehicle inspection only for TNC vehicles five years old or older.
michigan.tnc_statute: Limousine, Taxicab, and Transportation Network Company Act, 2016 PA 345, MCL 257.2101 et seq.; insurance requirements at MCL 257.2123
michigan.um_uim_note: Michigan's TNC statute (MCL 257.2123) does not require UM/UIM coverage, and UM/UIM is optional in Michigan generally; Uber and Lyft company policies do provide UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2-3, but that is a company benefit, not a state mandate.
michigan.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. In Periods 1-3 the required coverage may be held by the driver, the TNC, or both, and if the required insurance lapses or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar and defend the claim (MCL 257.2123(5)). TNC coverage is not dependent on the personal insurer denying the claim first (MCL 257.2123(6)), so a personal policy's commercial-use exclusion does not block the TNC policy. Michigan is a no-fault state, so an injured passenger usually claims PIP medical benefits from their own (or a resident relative's) policy first.

minnesota.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 for two or more persons bodily injury or death, $30,000 property damage
minnesota.period2_3_limits: $1,500,000 combined single limit for death, injury, or destruction of property of others, plus a separate TNC-provided personal-injury policy of at least $1,000,000 per incident for the driver
minnesota.sol_note: For a negligence crash claim, the clock runs 6 years from the crash under Minn. Stat. § 541.05, subd. 1(5); note that some secondary sources cite the 2-year period in § 541.07(1), which applies to intentional torts such as assault and battery, not ordinary negligence, and claims against a government entity have separate shorter notice rules.
minnesota.sources: Minn. Stat. § 65B.472, Minn. Stat. ch. 181C, Minn. Stat. § 541.05, Minn. Stat. § 65B.49
minnesota.state_note: Minnesota has the highest Period 2-3 liability minimum in this set at $1,500,000, not $1,000,000, and it is the only state here that also requires the TNC to provide a separate $1,000,000 personal-injury policy for the driver at no cost to the driver. Its 2024 TNC law (ch. 181C) also sets driver minimum pay and deactivation rules, enforced by the Department of Labor and Industry.
minnesota.tnc_statute: Minn. Stat. § 65B.472 (Transportation Network Financial Responsibility) and Minn. Stat. ch. 181C (Transportation Network Companies, enacted 2024)
minnesota.um_uim_note: Primary uninsured motorist and underinsured motorist coverage are required in Period 1 and in Periods 2-3 where required by Minn. Stat. § 65B.49, subdivisions 3a and 4a (Minn. Stat. § 65B.472, subd. 2(b)(3)), at Minnesota's statutory UM/UIM minimums.
minnesota.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. In Periods 1-3 the driver or the TNC on the driver's behalf must maintain primary insurance that expressly recognizes rideshare use. If the driver's coverage lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance steps in from the first dollar. Minnesota is a no-fault state, so basic economic loss (medical and wage-loss) benefits are also part of the required coverage in Period 1.

mississippi.agency_name: Mississippi Department of Insurance (licenses transportation network companies)
mississippi.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
mississippi.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage
mississippi.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash under Miss. Code § 15-1-49, with tolling for minors and persons under a legal disability, and a shorter deadline applies to claims against a government entity.
mississippi.sources: Miss. Code §§ 63-15-39 to 63-15-43, Miss. Code § 77-7-7, Miss. Code § 83-11-101, Mississippi Department of Insurance TNC insurance requirements (HB 1381), Miss. Code § 15-1-49
mississippi.state_note: Mississippi splits legal aid geographically: North Mississippi Rural Legal Services covers the northern counties and the Mississippi Center for Legal Services covers the central and southern counties, and both are reached through the statewide MSLegalServices.org portal. A TNC business-entity license in Mississippi carries a $5,000 annual fee.
mississippi.tnc_statute: Mississippi House Bill 1381 (2016), codified at Miss. Code §§ 63-15-39 to 63-15-43 (TNC insurance) and Miss. Code § 77-7-7 (TNC licensing)
mississippi.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both periods to the extent required by Miss. Code § 83-11-101; Mississippi requires UM coverage unless the insured rejects it in writing, at the statutory minimum limits.
mississippi.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC on the driver's behalf must maintain primary insurance that recognizes rideshare use, and the requirements may be met by the driver's policy, the TNC's policy, or a combination. Mississippi law expressly allows personal insurers to exclude coverage for losses while the driver is logged on or providing a prearranged ride, which is why the TNC's primary coverage is the payer in those periods.

missouri.agency_name: Missouri Department of Revenue, Motor Vehicle Bureau (licenses transportation network companies)
missouri.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
missouri.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury, and property damage
missouri.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the injury under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.120(4), with tolling for minors; a 2025 bill (HB 68) that would have cut this to 2 years for injuries after August 28, 2025 passed the House but died in the Senate, so the 5-year period still applies, while claims against a government entity require notice within 90 days.
missouri.sources: Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 387.400 to 387.440, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 379.1702, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.120(4), Missouri Department of Revenue TNC licensing page
missouri.state_note: Missouri has one of the longest personal-injury deadlines in the country at 5 years, and its TNC law expressly allows the Kansas City and St. Louis Regional Taxicab Commission to audit a licensed TNC up to twice a year. Missouri is also unusual in splitting TNC regulation (Department of Revenue licensing) from TNC insurance rules (chapter 379).
missouri.tnc_statute: Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 387.400 to 387.440 (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 379.1700 to 379.1708
missouri.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both Period 1 and Periods 2-3 in an amount not less than the limits in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 379.203 (RSMo § 379.1702(2)(2) and (3)(2)).
missouri.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC on the driver's behalf must maintain primary insurance that recognizes rideshare use. If the driver's insurance has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance provides it from the first dollar and defends the claim, and if the driver's policy covers the loss but below the required limits, the TNC provides excess coverage up to the required limits (RSMo § 379.1702(4)).

montana.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
montana.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for death, bodily injury, and property damage
montana.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash under Mont. Code Ann. § 27-2-204, with a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered and tolling for minors, and a shorter notice deadline applies to claims against a government entity.
montana.sources: Mont. Code Ann. §§ 69-12-341 to 69-12-345, Mont. Code Ann. § 27-2-204, Montana Public Service Commission motor carrier page
montana.state_note: Montana is distinctive in calling rideshare companies 'transportation network carriers' and regulating them as Class E motor carriers that must hold a certificate of compliance from the Public Service Commission, and state law expressly bars local governments from regulating TNC services. Montana Legal Services Association is the state's sole statewide provider of general civil legal assistance.
montana.tnc_statute: Mont. Code Ann. Title 69, chapter 12, §§ 69-12-341 to 69-12-345 (Transportation Network Carriers, Class E motor carriers; SB 396, 2015)
montana.um_uim_note: Montana's TNC statute (MCA 69-12-343) does not expressly require UM/UIM coverage; Montana law requires insurers to offer UM coverage, which a driver may reject, and Uber and Lyft company policies provide UM/UIM coverage during Periods 2-3, but that is a company benefit, not a state TNC mandate.
montana.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary insurance recognizing rideshare use, and if the driver's policy lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance must cover the claim from the first dollar and defend it (MCA 69-12-343). Personal insurers in Montana may exclude all coverage, including UM/UIM and collision, for losses while the driver is logged on or providing a prearranged ride (MCA 69-12-345).

nebraska.period1_limits: $25,000 per person / $50,000 per incident for death and personal injury, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured motorist coverage
nebraska.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, personal injury, and property damage, plus uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage of at least $1,000,000 for the driver and passengers
nebraska.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-207, with tolling for minors and a discovery rule for injuries that could not reasonably have been discovered, and claims against a government entity require a tort claim notice within 1 year.
nebraska.sources: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 75-321 to 75-341, Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 75-333 and 75-334, Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-207, 291 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 3, § 012
nebraska.state_note: Nebraska has the lowest Period 1 minimums in this set at $25,000/$50,000/$25,000, half the bodily-injury limits most other states require while waiting for a ride, while its engaged-stage UM/UIM requirement of $1,000,000 is among the strongest. Nebraska also uses its own stage names: application-open, engaged, and passengers-on-board.
nebraska.tnc_statute: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 75-321 to 75-341 (Transportation Network Company Act; LB 629, 2015); insurance at Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 75-333 and 75-334
nebraska.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in the application-open stage (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 75-334), and UM/UIM coverage of at least $1,000,000 for both driver and passengers is required in the engaged and passengers-on-board stages (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 75-333).
nebraska.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. In the application-open stage (logged on, no ride accepted) the TNC or driver must maintain primary TNC insurance, and in the engaged and passengers-on-board stages the TNC's $1,000,000 policy is primary. Nebraska's Department of Insurance warns that personal auto policies typically exclude business use or being available for hire, so a personal insurer's denial in those stages is expected and the TNC policy is the payer.

nevada.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per crash bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage
nevada.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 for bodily injury to or death of one or more persons and injury to or destruction of property of others in any one accident
nevada.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash under Nev. Rev. Stat. § 11.190(4)(e), with a discovery rule for latent injuries and tolling for minors, and claims against a government entity have a shorter notice and filing deadline.
nevada.sources: Nev. Rev. Stat. ch. 706A, Nev. Rev. Stat. § 690B.470, Nev. Rev. Stat. § 690B.480, 2025 Statutes of Nevada ch. 5 (AB 523), Nev. Rev. Stat. § 11.190(4)(e)
nevada.state_note: Nevada's trip-period minimum was $1,500,000 until AB 523 (2025) cut it to $1,000,000 effective October 1, 2025, so many older sources still quote $1,500,000 and the crash date decides which figure applies; the same 2025 law added NRS 706A.155 barring vicarious liability for TNCs. Nevada is also one of the few states here with no UM/UIM requirement at all in the rideshare context.
nevada.tnc_statute: Nev. Rev. Stat. ch. 706A (Transportation Network Companies); insurance requirements at Nev. Rev. Stat. § 690B.470
nevada.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is NOT required in Nevada's TNC insurance law; NRS 690B.470(6) says a TNC policy may include UM/UIM, medical payments, comprehensive and collision coverage, but none of it is required, and Uber and Lyft are reported not to provide UM/UIM coverage for drivers in Nevada.
nevada.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies, and Nevada's general minimums are $25,000/$50,000/$20,000. In Period 1 the TNC insurance is not contingent on the personal insurer denying first, and the TNC insurer has a duty to defend and indemnify (NRS 690B.470(7)-(8)). A personal insurer may exclude TNC activity entirely and then has no duty to defend or indemnify (NRS 690B.480), so the TNC policy is the payer once the driver is logged on.

new hampshire.agency_name: New Hampshire Department of Safety, Division of Motor Vehicles
new hampshire.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident for death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
new hampshire.period2_3_limits: $300,000 combined for death, bodily injury, and property damage under RSA 359-U:8; Uber and Lyft company policies provide $1,000,000 during this period, which is above the state minimum
new hampshire.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the act causing the injury under N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 508:4(I), or on discovery if the injury and its cause could not reasonably have been discovered then, with tolling for minors, and a shorter notice deadline applies to claims against a government entity.
new hampshire.sources: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. ch. 359-U, RSA 359-U:8, RSA 359-U:10, RSA 264:15, N.H. Admin. Rules Saf-C 5400, N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 508:4
new hampshire.state_note: New Hampshire is the outlier in this set: its statutory minimum for a prearranged ride is only $300,000, not $1,000,000, so the $1,000,000 figure riders see comes from Uber and Lyft company policies, not state law. It is also the only state here where most drivers are not required to carry auto insurance at all, which makes the TNC policy especially important.
new hampshire.tnc_statute: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. ch. 359-U (Transportation Network Company; RSA 376-A repealed and replaced by 2023 ch. 30, eff. July 1, 2023); insurance at RSA 359-U:8; rules at N.H. Admin. Rules Saf-C 5400
new hampshire.um_uim_note: RSA 359-U:8 does not expressly require UM/UIM coverage in the TNC policy, but any auto policy issued in New Hampshire must include UM coverage equal to the bodily-injury liability limits (RSA 264:15), and Uber provides $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage during a trip under its company policy.
new hampshire.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies, and New Hampshire is unusual in not requiring most drivers to carry auto insurance at all, only proof of financial responsibility. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage, and if the driver's insurance has lapsed or falls short, the TNC's insurance provides the required coverage from the first dollar and defends the claim (RSA 359-U:8). TNC coverage is not dependent on the personal insurer denying the claim first (RSA 359-U:8), and personal insurers may exclude all coverage during TNC activity (RSA 359-U:10).

new jersey.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus primary PIP
new jersey.period2_3_limits: $1,500,000 for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus at least $10,000 in medical payments per person for the driver and $1,500,000 in UM/UIM coverage
new jersey.sol_note: The clock starts when the claim accrues, normally the crash date, under N.J.S.A. 2A:14-2, with a discovery rule for injuries discovered later and tolling for minors, and claims against a public entity require a notice of claim within 90 days under the Tort Claims Act.
new jersey.sources: N.J.S.A. 39:5H-1 et seq., N.J.S.A. 39:5H-10, N.J.S.A. 39:5H-12, N.J.S.A. 17:28-1.1, N.J.S.A. 2A:14-2, New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission TNC FAQ
new jersey.state_note: New Jersey has the strongest rideshare insurance package in this set: $1,500,000 in liability and $1,500,000 in UM/UIM coverage in Periods 2-3, plus $10,000 in medical payments for the driver, and it is a no-fault state, so PIP applies in Period 1 as well. A New Jersey appeals court has also held that the TNC act covers transport of people, not app-based food delivery.
new jersey.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Company Safety and Regulatory Act, P.L.2017, c.26, N.J.S.A. 39:5H-1 et seq.; insurance at N.J.S.A. 39:5H-10
new jersey.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required in both stages: in Period 1 at the state minimum under N.J.S.A. 17:28-1.1 (now $35,000 per person / $70,000 per incident bodily injury and $25,000 property damage as of January 1, 2026), and in Periods 2-3 at least $1,500,000 (N.J.S.A. 39:5H-10).
new jersey.who_pays_note: When the app is off, only the driver's personal policy applies. While logged on or on a prearranged ride, the driver, the TNC, or a combination must maintain the required primary coverage, and the TNC's coverage is primary, not a backstop. If the driver's coverage lapses or falls short, the TNC's insurance must provide the required coverage from the first dollar. A New Jersey personal insurer may exclude any and all coverage while the driver is logged on or on a ride (N.J.S.A. 39:5H-12), so the TNC policy is the payer in those periods, and New Jersey's no-fault PIP system covers medical bills first.

new mexico.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage
new mexico.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary automobile liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
new mexico.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, is paused for minors until they turn 18, and a claim against a government entity faces a much shorter 90-day notice deadline under the New Mexico Tort Claims Act.
new mexico.sources: NMSA 1978 Section 65-7-8 (Justia), Transportation Network Company Services Act (nmlegis.gov), 18.7.1 NMAC (srca.nm.gov), NMSA 1978 Section 37-1-8
new mexico.state_note: Regulation of TNCs moved from the Public Regulation Commission to the Department of Transportation on July 1, 2024, under the current version of 18.7.1 NMAC.
new mexico.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Company Services Act, NMSA 1978 Sections 65-7-1 to 65-7-22 (insurance requirements at Section 65-7-8)
new mexico.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required to the extent required by NMSA 1978 Section 66-5-301, which requires insurers to offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage equal to the bodily injury limits; it applies in both Period 1 and during a prearranged ride unless the driver rejected it in writing.
new mexico.who_pays_note: While the app is off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. Once the driver is logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, and Uber/Lyft provide contingent coverage in Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's personal policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance steps in as the primary coverage, and New Mexico law expressly allows personal auto insurers to exclude coverage while the car is used for rideshare.

new york.agency_name: New York State Department of Financial Services
new york.period1_limits: $75,000 per person / $150,000 per accident bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured motorist coverage and personal injury protection (no-fault)
new york.period2_3_limits: $1,250,000 liability for bodily injury, death and property damage, plus $1,250,000 supplemental uninsured/underinsured motorist (SUM) coverage and personal injury protection (no-fault)
new york.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, but a no-fault (PIP) claim must be filed within 30 days of the crash, and a claim against a city or other government body requires a notice of claim within 90 days.
new york.sources: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 1693, NY Department of Financial Services TNC FAQ (dfs.ny.gov), CPLR Section 214
new york.state_note: New York's limits are the highest in this group outside New York City ($1,250,000 per trip), but Article 44-B does not apply to trips originating in New York City, where Uber and Lyft cars are for-hire vehicles under Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) rules requiring at least $100,000/$300,000 bodily injury coverage.
new york.tnc_statute: Vehicle and Traffic Law Article 44-B, Transportation Network Company Services, Sections 1691-1699 (insurance requirements at Section 1693)
new york.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in Period 1, and during a prearranged trip the policy must include $1,250,000 in supplemental uninsured/underinsured motorist (SUM) coverage — far above the $25,000 minimum UM coverage on a regular New York auto policy.
new york.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at New York's $25,000/$50,000 minimums plus $50,000 no-fault PIP. Once logged on, the TNC must maintain a group policy that satisfies the limits above, and that TNC coverage is primary; a personal insurer's rideshare exclusion does not defeat the TNC coverage. No-fault PIP pays medical bills and lost wages first regardless of fault, and a claim for pain and suffering still requires a 'serious injury' under Insurance Law Section 5102(d).

north carolina.agency_name: North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles
north carolina.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
north carolina.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
north carolina.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, or when a hidden injury is or should have been discovered, with a 10-year outer limit; the period is paused while the injured person is a minor.
north carolina.sources: N.C.G.S. Sections 20-280.3 and 20-280.4 (ncleg.gov), N.C.G.S. Section 1-52, NC Division of Motor Vehicles TNC permit packet (ncshp.gov)
north carolina.state_note: North Carolina is one of the few states that still uses contributory negligence, so any fault on the injured person's part, no matter how small, can bar recovery entirely. TNCs must get a permit from the Division of Motor Vehicles and renew it annually.
north carolina.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Companies Act, N.C.G.S. Article 10A, Sections 20-280.1 to 20-280.10 (insurance requirements at Section 20-280.4)
north carolina.um_uim_note: Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is required with the TNC policy under North Carolina's mandatory UM law; during Periods 2-3 Uber and Lyft carry $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage, and in Period 1 UM/UIM follows the state's mandatory uninsured motorist requirements.
north carolina.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. In Period 1, Uber and Lyft provide contingent liability coverage that only pays if the driver's personal policy denies the claim or is exhausted, which is where most coverage disputes arise. Once a ride is accepted, the TNC's $1,000,000 policy is primary, and the driver's personal insurer may exclude rideshare use entirely.

north dakota.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
north dakota.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
north dakota.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash and is paused for minors until age 18, but a wrongful-death claim has a shorter 2-year deadline.
north dakota.sources: N.D.C.C. Chapters 39-34 and 26.1-40.1, 2023 HB 1440 (ndlegis.gov), N.D.C.C. Section 28-01-16(5)
north dakota.state_note: North Dakota's 6-year personal injury deadline is among the longest in the country, and its no-fault PIP system means medical bills are paid through PIP regardless of fault. TNCs and drivers are governed exclusively by Chapters 39-34 and 26.1-40.1, and cities may not add their own TNC rules.
north dakota.tnc_statute: Transportation Company Networks, N.D.C.C. Chapter 39-34, and TNC insurance, N.D.C.C. Chapter 26.1-40.1 (Sections 26.1-40.1-03 and 26.1-40.1-04), as amended by 2023 HB 1440
north dakota.um_uim_note: UM and UIM coverage must meet the requirements of N.D.C.C. Sections 26.1-40-15.2 and 26.1-40-15.3 and is primary coverage during an engaged or on-board ride; personal injury protection (PIP) under Chapter 26.1-41 is also required for drivers, passengers and pedestrians.
north dakota.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. Once logged on, the TNC or the driver must maintain TNC insurance, and the $1,000,000 policy is primary once a ride is accepted. Under a 2023 change, TNC coverage may not depend on the driver's personal insurer first denying the claim, and if the personal policy does not cover the loss the TNC policy pays from the first dollar.

ohio.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage
ohio.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for bodily injury or death and property damage in any one accident
ohio.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, is paused for minors until they turn 18, and a claim involving a government vehicle usually requires prompt notice and faces shorter deadlines.
ohio.sources: Ohio Revised Code Sections 3942.02, 4925.02 and 4925.10 (codes.ohio.gov), Ohio Revised Code Section 2305.10(A)
ohio.state_note: Ohio law makes TNCs pay and defend claims when a driver fails to maintain the required coverage, and drivers are independent contractors, not employees, under Ohio Revised Code Section 4925.10, so the TNC generally cannot be sued under respondeat superior for a driver's negligence.
ohio.tnc_statute: Ohio Revised Code Chapter 4925 (Transportation Network Companies) and Chapter 3942 (TNC insurance, Section 3942.02)
ohio.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is not required by Ohio law — it is optional in Ohio and the TNC statute does not mandate it — though Uber's and Lyft's own $1,000,000 policies include uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage during Periods 2-3.
ohio.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at Ohio's $25,000/$50,000/$25,000 minimums. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, with Uber/Lyft providing contingent coverage in Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's personal policy does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar, and the TNC may not require the personal insurer to deny the claim first; personal insurers may exclude all coverage while the driver is logged on.

oklahoma.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage
oklahoma.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
oklahoma.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash (or when the injury is discovered); minors get extra time, and a claim involving a government vehicle requires a written notice to the government within 1 year under the Governmental Tort Claims Act.
oklahoma.sources: 47 O.S. Section 1025 (oklegislature.gov), Oklahoma Transportation Network Company Services Act 47 O.S. Sections 1010-1030, 12 O.S. Section 95(A)(3)
oklahoma.state_note: A bill introduced in the 2026 session (HB 4357) would double the Period 1 minimums to $100,000 per person / $200,000 per incident / $50,000 property damage, but it has not passed, so the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 limits remain the law.
oklahoma.tnc_statute: Oklahoma Transportation Network Company Services Act, 47 O.S. Sections 1010-1030 (insurance requirements at Section 1025)
oklahoma.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both Period 1 and during a prearranged ride unless the driver waived it in writing under 36 O.S. Section 3636; the minimum UM limits track Oklahoma's $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident minimums.
oklahoma.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at Oklahoma's $25,000/$50,000/$25,000 minimums. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, with the platform's policy covering Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's personal policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance provides it from the first dollar, and personal auto policies typically exclude liability while carrying passengers for a fee.

oregon.agency_name: Portland Bureau of Transportation (Private For-Hire Transportation program)
oregon.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage (Portland City Code Section 16.40.230; no statewide tiered minimum exists)
oregon.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 combined single limit primary liability (Portland City Code Section 16.40.230; no statewide tiered minimum exists)
oregon.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered, with a 10-year outer limit under ORS 12.115; a claim against a government body needs a tort-claim notice within 180 days.
oregon.sources: ORS 742.518, 742.520 and 742.502, Portland City Code Sections 16.40.230 and 16.40.010 (portland.gov), ORS 12.110(1)
oregon.state_note: Oregon is unusual in having no comprehensive statewide TNC law: the only statewide TNC-specific statute requires PIP benefits, and permits, background checks and the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 and $1,000,000 insurance tiers are set by individual cities, with Portland's Chapter 16.40 as the model. Oregon uses modified comparative fault with a 51% bar under ORS 31.600.
oregon.tnc_statute: Oregon Revised Statutes Sections 742.518 and 742.520 (TNC personal injury protection, HB 2393 of 2021); Portland City Code Chapter 16.40, Section 16.40.230 (insurance tiers) — Oregon has no statewide TNC operating statute
oregon.um_uim_note: Oregon law (ORS 742.502) requires UM/UIM coverage equal to the bodily injury liability limits on every auto policy, including TNC coverage; the statewide TNC law also requires personal injury protection of at least $15,000 in medical expenses plus up to $3,000 per month in wage loss for up to 52 weeks for drivers, passengers and pedestrians struck by the vehicle.
oregon.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. In Portland, the TNC must maintain primary coverage for all periods, with the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 tier while waiting and $1,000,000 once a ride is accepted, so there is no coverage gap. Outside Portland there is no statewide tiered liability law, so coverage depends on the city, the TNC's own policy, and whether the driver's personal policy has a livery exclusion, which can leave a gap in Period 1.

pennsylvania.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus first-party medical benefits of $25,000 for pedestrians and $5,000 for the driver
pennsylvania.period2_3_limits: $500,000 primary automobile liability for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus first-party medical benefits of $25,000 for passengers and pedestrians
pennsylvania.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered; minors have until 2 years after turning 18, and a claim against a government body needs written notice within 6 months.
pennsylvania.sources: 66 Pa.C.S. Section 2603.1 (legis.state.pa.us), 53 Pa.C.S. Section 57A07, PA PUC TNC page (puc.pa.gov), 42 Pa.C.S. Section 5524(2)
pennsylvania.state_note: Pennsylvania's statutory trip minimum is only $500,000, not $1,000,000 as many secondary sources claim — the $1,000,000 figure is the companies' own policy limit, not the state floor. Chapter 26 does not apply inside a city of the first class, so rides in Philadelphia are regulated by the Philadelphia Parking Authority under 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 57A.
pennsylvania.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Service, 66 Pa.C.S. Chapter 26, Sections 2601-2605 (insurance requirements at Section 2603.1); Philadelphia is governed separately by 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 57A, Section 57A07
pennsylvania.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is not required by Pennsylvania law — it is optional and the TNC statute does not require it — though Uber's and Lyft's own policies typically include UM/UIM coverage during a trip; the $500,000 statutory trip minimum is lower than the companies' own $1,000,000 policies.
